papers.title: [Editorial] Rethinking lived experience
papers.summary: The theme of this year's World Mental Health Day, held on Oct 10, is Lived experiences heard: real voices, real change. On its website, WHO states that the voices of people with lived experience should “shape the policies, services and decisions that affect their lives”. While these are laudable aims, they also serve to highlight the complex challenges involved in lived experience engagement and co-production, both within the field of mental health and beyond.

papers.title: [Comment] Retatrutide in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes: what have we learned from TRIUMPH-2?
papers.summary: It is a general observation that the degree of weight loss obtained with GLP-1 receptor agonists is less in individuals with type 2 diabetes than in people without diabetes and similar BMI. Could this difference be overcome with the new triple agonists with superior weight-lowering effects? The TRIUMPH-2 study by Virginia Bellido and colleagues1 in The Lancet is a double-blind, parallel-group, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial of the effects of retatrutide, a triple agonist (GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon), in people with obesity and type 2 diabetes.

papers.title: [Comment] Adjuvant radiotherapy for atypical meningioma
papers.summary: Surgical resection remains the mainstay of treatment for atypical meningiomas, corresponding to WHO grade 2 tumours, particularly given the substantial risk of recurrence after subtotal resection. Accordingly, adjuvant radiotherapy has been proposed as a means of reducing the risk of recurrence, and its role is relatively well accepted in patients with residual tumour. After gross total resection (defined as Simpson grade I–III), however, the rationale is less clear: 5-year progression-free survival with gross total resection alone is 67–86%, and the role of adjuvant radiotherapy remains controversial, with its benefit in disease control weighed against potential toxicities.

papers.title: [Comment] Closing the gap on mortality for adolescents living with HIV
papers.summary: Despite major advancements in antiretroviral therapy (ART), a substantial mortality gap remains for adolescents living with HIV compared with the general population.1 Adolescents’ access to ART lags behind that of adults—approximately 60% for adolescents compared with 78% overall.2 For those who do receive life-saving therapy, inconsistent adherence to daily ART among many adolescents with HIV leads to viral non-suppression, increasing risks of clinical failure and death.3 The LATA trial, reported in The Lancet by Mutsa Bwakura-Dangarembizi and colleagues, was conducted in the four African countries in which most of the world's 1·57 million adolescents living with HIV reside; it offers hope that the challenges of adhering to daily oral ART for adolescents can be mitigated with longer acting injectable treatment options.

papers.title: [Comment] The arts belong at the heart of health policy
papers.summary: As Chile's Minister of Health from 2000 to 2002, I ran a public network that shortened waiting lists and expanded primary care, although it could not repair what fear, isolation, and broken trust do to a population. As the first female President in my country (2006–10 and 2014–18), I signed into law the Ministry of Cultures, the Arts, and Heritage, giving Chile's cultural life its first cabinet-level home. These experiences taught me that a country's cultural life and its health are the same project, seen from two angles.

papers.title: [Comment] Offline: Medicine for peace
papers.summary: Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) is most famous for his line in Leviathan (1651) that, “the life of man, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short”. That proposition may have been true in 17th-century England, but, thanks to the evolution and expansion of health systems, it is not so today for many, although obviously not all. But abstracting that line alone is to miss Hobbes’ wider views about the nature of human being. He believed that without a “common power” ruling over society, our natural tendency is “that condition which is called war…of every man against every man”.

papers.summary: Changes to the formulary for 14 000 prisoners have been criticised as inconsistent with best practice. Paul Webster reports.

papers.title: [World Report] Scabies in the south Pacific
papers.summary: Countries such as the Solomon Islands and Fiji have pioneered mass drug administration for the disease. Sophie Cousins reports.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Declare the climate crisis a Public Health Emergency of International Concern
papers.summary: Climate change is shaping health in the 21st century. In the past few weeks alone, Nepal has faced unprecedented flash floods, and multiple countries have experienced deadly heatwaves and catastrophic wildfires.1 El Niño is now firmly established and projected to intensify further.2 The southern hemisphere faces a summer of extreme heatwaves, droughts, and floods, threatening maternal and child health in particular, and increasing infectious disease outbreaks.3 Populations in lower-income countries bear a disproportionate burden of these impacts, but are least responsible for emissions and have few resources to respond.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Regulate prospective development of medical AI now
papers.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is advancing through medicine at a pace that regulation, ethics, and professional reflection have struggled to match. The prevailing assumption appears to be that if a technology can be developed, it should be developed—and that its place in clinical care can be debated afterwards. We believe this sequence should be reversed.

papers.title: [Correspondence] The health literacy crisis in the age of AI: lessons from PISA 2025
papers.summary: The 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) results should concern the health community.1 PISA does not measure health literacy directly, but it assesses several cognitive competencies that increasingly underpin people's ability to navigate health information. For example, in 2025, more than 760 000 students aged 15 years, from 91 countries and economies, participated in the assessment.1 The findings reveal a worrying deterioration in reading, mathematics, and science performance.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Taiwan's path to hepatitis C elimination
papers.summary: WHO has established a global target to eliminate viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030.1 Chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection remains one of the leading causes of cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and liver-related mortality, affecting an estimated 50 million people worldwide.2 By integrating a comprehensive screening-to-cure cascade, HCV elimination has become an achievable public health goal.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Personalising maintenance after tirzepatide weight loss
papers.summary: Deborah B Horn and colleagues’ SURMOUNT-MAINTAIN trial provides important evidence that continued tirzepatide is superior to treatment withdrawal for maintaining pharmacologically induced weight loss.1 The trial also shows that reducing tirzepatide to 5 mg offers substantially greater protection against weight regain than switching to placebo. However, the trial's mean effects might not fully convey an important clinical message: response to lower-dose maintenance was heterogeneous.

papers.title: [Correspondence] How much can ASTRUM-006 tell us?
papers.summary: Lin Shen and colleagues report improved event-free survival with perioperative serplulimab in PD-L1-positive resectable gastric or gastro-oesophageal junction adenocarcinoma.1 The trial is valuable: it selects patients by combined positive score and tests a chemotherapy-free adjuvant phase. However, we urge caution before it is read as practice-changing.

papers.title: [Correspondence] How much can ASTRUM-006 tell us? – Authors’ reply
papers.summary: We thank Osman Bilge Kaya and Berkan Karabuğa for their insightful comments regarding ASTRUM-006.1 We agree that some aspects need further clarification.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Colonoscopy screening and colorectal cancer outcomes: the NordICC trial
papers.summary: Michal F Kaminski and colleagues report that colonoscopy screening reduced colorectal cancer incidence, but not mortality, during a 13-year follow-up.1 The response from the public health field will focus, as it always does, on mortality. We think this focus misses the point of the trial.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Colonoscopy screening and colorectal cancer outcomes: the NordICC trial
papers.summary: In their recent Article, Michal F Kaminski and colleagues reported the effects of offering one-time screening colonoscopy at ages 55–64 years after a 13-year follow-up of the NordICC trial.1 Their findings should be interpreted in the context that this trial of a one-time offer of screening colonoscopy was conducted in an era of widespread use of colonoscopy in clinical practice. Estimated reductions in the incidence and mortality of colorectal cancer were much lower than anticipated at trial design.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Colonoscopy screening and colorectal cancer outcomes: the NordICC trial
papers.summary: The NordICC trial1 should be considered in context with previous colorectal cancer screening studies.2,3 Four randomised controlled trials with more than 458 000 participants show consistent colorectal cancer incidence reductions of 18–23% and larger colorectal cancer mortality reductions of 22–31% with sigmoidoscopy (appendix).3 In the NordICC trial, screening reduced colorectal cancer incidence but not mortality.1

papers.title: [Correspondence] Colonoscopy screening and colorectal cancer outcomes: the NordICC trial – Authors’ reply
papers.summary: We thank João Martins and Aneel Bhangu, Hermann Brenner and colleagues, and Uri Ladabaum and colleagues for their interesting comments on our report from the NordICC trial.1 We agree with Martins and Bhangu that colorectal cancer incidence is an interesting primary target for preventive screening tests, such as colonoscopy. The effect on cancer incidence is one of the advantages of preventive screening tests, compared with early detection screening tests (eg, breast cancer screening with mammography or prostate cancer screening with prostate-specific antigen).

papers.title: [Articles] Retatrutide in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes (TRIUMPH-2): a double-blind, parallel-group, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial
papers.summary: Treatment with retatrutide resulted in substantial improvements in bodyweight and was associated with improvements in glycaemic control in participants with obesity and type 2 diabetes, with a safety profile generally consistent with other molecules with GLP-1 receptor agonism. These results show that retatrutide might be effective for the treatment of obesity in people with type 2 diabetes.

papers.title: [Articles] Radiotherapy versus observation following surgical resection of WHO grade 2 atypical meningioma (ROAM/EORTC-1308): an international, multicentre, open-label, phase 3, randomised controlled trial
papers.summary: Our findings suggest that adjuvant radiotherapy should be considered in patients with atypical meningioma after complete surgical resection of atypical meningioma when the prevention of recurrence is valued higher than the potential delayed adverse effects of radiotherapy. This practice will benefit patients by reducing meningioma recurrence. Decisions should be based on individual discussion with the patient.

papers.title: [Articles] Switch to injectable cabotegravir–rilpivirine given every 8 weeks in adolescents living with HIV with virological suppression in sub-Saharan Africa (LATA): a randomised, open-label, multicentre, 96-week non-inferiority trial
papers.summary: In adolescents with HIV with virological suppression, LAI cabotegravir–rilpivirine was superior to TLD for maintaining virological suppression, with no new safety concerns observed. These findings support LAI cabotegravir–rilpivirine as a maintenance treatment option for this population.

papers.title: [Review] Developing roadmaps for advancing practice, research, and policy in the arts and health
papers.summary: Despite arts engagement being a ubiquitous human behaviour across human history, research and awareness on the health benefits of engagement are still emerging, accelerating over the past decade. Building on the evidence and research challenges outlined in the first paper of this Lancet collection, this Review puts forward a series of roadmaps for advancing research, policy, and practice to enable appropriate and effective integration of the arts into health and wellbeing systems globally. First and foremost, we advocate for the fundamental principle that all individuals, regardless of their characteristics and location, should have regular opportunities to engage in the arts, proposing policy and research steps to monitor and achieve this goal.

papers.title: [Editorial] Counteracting the rise of antimicrobial resistance in Shigella
papers.summary: Shigella, a Gram-negative bacterium, causes shigellosis, characterised by intestinal symptoms. Shigellosis is one of the leading causes of global diarrhoeal disease deaths, especially in children younger than 5 years. Shigella disproportionately affects low-income and middle-income countries (LMICs), where transmission occurs mainly through the oral–faecal route due to poor water, sanitation, and hygiene practices. Shigella is divided into four main species: S dysenteriae, S boydii, S flexneri, and S sonnei, of which all have multiple serotypes except S flexneri.

papers.title: [News] Infection prevention and control gaps in Pakistan
papers.summary: Clusters of HIV infections in children caused by unsafe injection practices in hospitals in Pakistan continue to occur. Talha Burki reports.

papers.title: [News] Research in brief
papers.summary: A cohort study in France assessed the monoclonal antibody nirsevimab against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in infants at 1 year and 2 years after immunisation. Outcomes were examined in infants born before the first RSVpreF vaccination campaign for pregnant women started in September 2024. Nirsevimab was associated with lower rates of RSV-lower respiratory tract-related hospitalisations during the first year after immunisation: 299 (0·8%) of 37 366 immunised versus 899 (2·4%) of 37 366 non-immunised infants in 2023, and 456 (0·5%) of 87 763 immunised versus 1711 (1.9%) of 87 763 non-immunised infants in 2024 (weighted hazard ratios 0·34, 95% CI 0·30–0·39 for the 2023 cohort and 0·28, 0.25–0·31 for the 2024 cohort, corresponding to nirsevimab effectiveness estimates of 66% and 72%, respectively).

papers.title: [Obituary] Bruce Ribner
papers.summary: Pioneering infectious disease physician and epidemiologist died on July 19, 2026, aged 80 years.

papers.title: [Profile] Mahboubeh Hajiabdolbaghi—advancing ID care in Iran
papers.summary: Mahboubeh Hajiabdolbaghi was born and raised in Tehran, where her parents encouraged education, curiosity, and independence. She studied medicine at Tehran University of Medical Sciences (TUMS), at a time when only around one in ten medical students was female. “The passion for learning my mother and father gave me has stayed with me throughout my life”, she tells The Lancet Infectious Diseases. She retired as Professor of Infectious Diseases at TUMS in 2022 and but continues in clinical practice in Tehran.

papers.title: [Clinical Picture] Lymphoma-like endoscopic appearance of lymphogranuloma venereum
papers.summary: A 34-year-old man with HIV who had sex with men was referred to our hospital after experiencing bloody mucoid stools for 6 months. He had initially presented to a local clinic, where haemorrhoids were suspected and topical treatment was prescribed. However, because his symptoms persisted, he was referred for further investigation. Colonoscopy revealed a circumferential 50 mm volcano-like rectal ulcer with an irregular, thick heaped-up margin and a deep ulcer base (figure A), accompanied by a smaller shallow round ulcer.

papers.title: Mapping transcriptional responses to cellular perturbations with RNA fingerprinting
papers.summary: RNA fingerprinting is a statistical framework that infers causal regulators from single-cell experiments by mapping their transcriptional responses onto reference perturbation dictionaries.

papers.title: A fluctuation test for gastruloid heterogeneity
papers.summary: Organoids grown side by side under identical conditions vary unpredictably, a longstanding obstacle to their use. Adapting the logic of a classic fluctuation test to gastruloids grown from single stem cells shows that this variability is largely inherited rather than induced and is traceable to fluctuations in the state of the founding cell.

papers.title: Comprehensive lineage tracing maps the landscape of cell fate decisions in mouse embryogenesis
papers.summary: We use PEtracer to reconstruct high-resolution lineage histories for >1.4 million cells from E7.5 to E10.0 during mouse development, providing a quantitative view of fate bias, restriction timing, and clonal output. Across diverse tissues, these data reveal highly reproducible lineage architectures and define general and tissue-specific strategies of cell fate specification.

papers.title: Immunoregulatory gene GIMAP6 suppresses lethal atherosclerotic vasculopathy and ischemic heart failure
papers.summary: By destabilizing the endothelium and promoting macrophage lipid loading and inflammation, GIMAP6 deficiency drives atherosclerosis and ischemic heart disease through a mechanism that operates without hyperlipidemia, yet hyperlipidemia significantly exacerbates disease progression.

papers.title: Arabidopsis uses distinct coumarins and bacterial pathways for pH-adaptive iron acquisition
papers.summary: Arabidopsis coordinates Fe acquisition with its root microbiota by releasing distinct coumarin chemotypes in response to environmental pH. These root-exuded specialized metabolites interact with root-associated bacteria to mobilize Fe either through bacterial siderophore-dependent chelation at circumneutral pH or through bacterial redox-sensing-controlled reduction at acidic pH.

papers.title: STING reprogramming by estrogen promotes neutrophil extracellular trap formation and sex-biased resistance to ADC therapy
papers.summary: Sex differences in antibody-based cancer therapy remain poorly understood. This study identifies estrogen-driven STING reprogramming and neutrophil extracellular trap formation as a mechanism of functional antigen shielding that limits ADC efficacy.

papers.title: A non-canonical function of glutathione to suppress ferroptosis via FSP1
papers.summary: Glutathione (GSH) robustly defends against ferroptosis independently of GPX4. FSP1 utilizes GSH to reduce ubiquinone and subsequently inhibits ferroptosis, which is distinct from the NAD(P)H-FAD axis. Targeting the FSP1-GSH axis efficiently alleviated ferroptosis-induced tissue injury.

papers.title: A spatiotemporal lifecycle atlas decodes spatial coordination in rice
papers.summary: A 3D spatiotemporal cell atlas of rice spanning the entire seed-to-seed lifecycle. Developmental trajectories are captured, and the spatially distinct roles of OsARF1 in rice development and dorsoventral endosperm asymmetry related to starch and protein accumulation are revealed.

papers.title: SPARCS enables scalable recovery of complex image-based phenotypes for genetic screening
papers.summary: Current genetic screens face a trade-off between scaling to large mutant libraries and measuring information-rich phenotypes. SPARCS automates laser microdissection to enable pooled forward genetic screens for complex image-based phenotypes at scale. By physically recovering individual mutants, SPARCS supports multimodal profiling of hits beyond genotyping, including via mass spectrometry-based proteomics.

papers.title: Cancer competition for vitamin B2 creates metabolic checkpoint for T cell ferroptosis
papers.summary: A CRISPR screen of solute carriers reveals that T cells depend on SLC52A3 for VB2 uptake, whereas tumors preferentially exploit SLC52A2 to outcompete them, thereby driving T cell ferroptosis. Enforced SLC52A3 overexpression in T cells reverses this metabolic competition and enhances their antitumor activity.

Salicylic acid engages central metabolic regulators SnRK1 and TOR to govern immunity by differential phosphorylation of NPR1
papers.summary: The immune signal SA triggers metabolic changes to activate SnRK1 while inhibiting TOR. These central metabolic kinases antagonistically phosphorylate the key immune regulator NPR1, thereby coupling cellular metabolic state to systemic acquired resistance.

papers.title: Gut microbiota primes stroke severity via the AHR in intestinal dendritic cells
papers.summary: Indole-producing Escherichia coli worsens ischemic stroke through the activation of aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling in dendritic cells. Limiting AHR signaling in DCs promotes gut-derived DC migration to the meninges, expands meningeal regulatory T cells, and reduces neuroinflammation. This microbiota-AHR axis offers a promising therapeutic target.

papers.title: Spatial evolution of a cachexia-promoting microenvironment in pancreatic cancer
papers.summary: Pancreatic cancer cachexia is accompanied by progressive assembly of a spatially organized tumor-macrophage-fibroblast niche. Reciprocal signaling among the cellular populations in the niche is associated with muscle wasting and cachexia progression.

papers.title: Microbiome signatures linked to cancer and treatment adverse events in a real-world cohort
papers.summary: In a large, real-world mixed-cancer cohort, analyses accounting for comorbidities and additional confounders indicate that most microbiome alterations are shared across cancers rather than specific to individual cancers. Distinct associations are limited to a subset of cancers and, in separate analyses, to age of onset and specific treatment-related adverse events.

papers.title: Cargo crosslinking nucleates AP-1 lattice formation
papers.summary: Cargo has traditionally been viewed as a passive substrate of coat-mediated transport. Cryo-EM reveals that cargo containing tandem sorting motifs directly promotes higher-order adaptor assembly by bridging AP-1 complexes, enabling efficient trafficking and neuronal development in zebrafish.

papers.title: Non-invasive control of gene editing in vivo by photoswitchable Cas12f and focused ultrasound
papers.summary: Remote activation of a single-AAV-deliverable photoswitchable Cas12f system enables precise spatial and temporal control of genome editing in deep tissues without surgery or implanted devices.

papers.title: Opposing functions of gut immunomodulatory metabolites on CAR-T therapy
papers.summary: Gut microbial taxonomy alone is a poor predictor of CAR-T cell therapy outcome. Instead, specific gut immunomodulatory metabolites exert opposing effects on CAR-T cell function and tumor control, identifying microbial metabolism as a potential target to predict and improve CAR-T cell outcomes.

papers.title: In-cell discovery and characterization of a non-canonical bacterial protein translocation-folding complex
papers.summary: In-cell cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) combined with proteomics, integrative structural modeling, and bioinformatics enables discovery and functional annotation of uncharacterized proteins. In the minimal bacterium Mycoplasma pneumoniae, this reveals a complex that links Sec-based protein translocation and extracellular folding, capable of supporting both co- and post-translational pathways.

papers.title: Single-cell visual proteomics of a minimal bacterium reveals structural coordination of gene expression machineries
papers.summary: Cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) resolves and quantifies an almost complete view of bacterial translation, revealing how gene expression machineries coordinate across the processes of transcription, translation, and membrane engagement directly within a minimal bacterium.

papers.title: Resident tissue macrophages transfer selenium transporter protein to protect pancreatic cancer from ferroptosis
papers.summary: Resident tissue macrophages establish a selenium-rich niche at the pancreatic tumor border and protect invading tumor cells from ferroptosis by transferring Selenop protein to EMThi cancer cells.

papers.title: A pericyte-to-myofibroblast transition links APOE4 to cerebrovascular degeneration
papers.summary: APOE4 causes a pericyte-to-myofibroblast transition that promotes cerebrovascular fibrosis and perivascular amyloid accumulation. TGF-β inhibition reverses this pathological remodeling and thus presents a therapeutic strategy to restore cerebrovascular homeostasis in these high-risk individuals.

papers.title: Shifts in embryonic oxygen levels cue heterochrony in limb initiation
papers.summary: Mammalian embryos see a substantial increase in available oxygen once the placenta forms. This increase in oxygen exposure serves as a trigger for initiating the development of the hindlimb, thus controlling developmental timing and, more broadly, linking the maternal environment to evolutionary changes in body plan.

papers.title: Microbial signaling coordinates group oviposition and predator defense in migratory locusts
papers.summary: This study reveals an egg-associated bacterial signaling mechanism that couples reproductive synchronization with offspring defense in the locust L. migratoria, expanding the functional landscape of insect-microbe-predator interactions and demonstrating how microbial signals can shape complex ecological behaviors.

papers.title: Direct cell-to-cell transmission of retrotransposons
papers.summary: Retrotransposons can infect neighboring cells using a mechanism that relies on a small fusogen-like protein rather than on the envelope protein that is typically required for infection.

papers.title: Projection-defined modules reveal mouse motor cortex architecture
papers.summary: The mouse motor cortex divides into 16 spatially organized modules based on distinct subcortical projections. This specificity covaries with cortical connectivity patterns and cell-type composition along two spatial axes, thereby defining the rules by which motor cortex modules integrate with granularity into brainwide and precisely wired neuronal networks to influence movement.

papers.title: CD4 T cells convert transient responses to KRAS inhibition to durable remissions in pancreatic cancer
papers.summary: An AI-designed IL-21 mimetic converts transient KRAS inhibitor responses into durable pancreatic cancer remissions through CD4 T cells, independent of CD8 T cells and tumor MHC class I expression.

papers.title: Switching of transcriptional control from interferon regulatory factor 2 to interferon regulatory factor 1 drives innate immune cell activation
papers.summary: Toll-like receptor signaling activates proinflammatory interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) even in the absence of interferon by triggering a shift from IRF2 to IRF1 occupancy at ISG promoters and enhancers. Newly translated IRF1 promotes proteasomal degradation of the weaker transcriptional activator IRF2 by engaging the E3 ubiquitin ligase SPOP.

papers.title: Chloroplasts balance energy production and stress resilience via a cold-induced signaling pathway
papers.summary: Cold-stress signals are transmitted to chloroplasts and subsequently trigger cold responses through an RAF-like bi-kinase module where cytoplasmic RAF3 and plasma membrane RAF6 translocate to chloroplasts, where they inhibit photosynthetic activity but activate nuclear cold-responsive gene expression.

papers.title: mRNA-encoding CD19-targeting T cell engager for refractory immune thrombocytopenia
papers.summary: An mRNA-lipid nanoparticle-encoded CD19×CD3 T cell engager depletes B cells with attenuated cytokine release in preclinical models. In three patients with treatment-refractory immune thrombocytopenia, treatment with this T cell engager achieved sustained platelet recovery over 6 months, suggesting that mRNA-encoded T cell engagers represent a promising therapeutic approach for resetting autoreactive immunity in B cell-driven autoimmune disease.

papers.title: Toward autonomous science with agentic artificial intelligence
papers.summary: Biomedical artificial intelligence is advancing from tools that answer human-posed questions to agents that ask their own. Guo et al. assess this transition, including scaling logic, autonomous-laboratory trajectory, and the risks of hallucination, bias, dual use, and cognitive deskilling. This perspective argues that progress depends on responsible human-AI collaboration.

papers.title: Phosphate backbone epitranscriptomics: Discovery of natural RNA phosphorothioates and their writer machinery
papers.summary: Phosphorothioates, stereospecific modifications of the RNA phosphate backbone in anaerobic archaea, expand the epitranscriptome beyond nucleobases and ribose sugars. Installed by Esti enzymes at conserved rRNA and tRNA hotspots, these environmentally responsive marks stabilize tRNAs and support growth at high temperatures.

papers.title: 3D chromatin remodeling during domestication defines novel targets for crop improvement
papers.summary: Population-level 3D genome atlas of 34 semi-wild and 267 cultivated allotetraploid cottons reveals domestication-selected chromatin conformations that enhance cotton fiber quality and unlock cryptic breeding targets.

papers.title: Gliomas phenocopy an inborn error of metabolism to drive neuronal activity and tumor growth
papers.summary: Glioma-derived guanidinoacetate depolarizes neighboring neurons through γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) A receptors, and depleting this metabolite reduces both neuronal activity and glioma growth.

papers.title: Single-cell-resolved genome atlas of prokaryoplankton inhabiting the ocean’s interior
papers.summary: GORG-Dark presents genomes of 9,698 individual bacterial and archaeal cells from the ocean’s sunless interior. The atlas resolves depth stratification to abyssal waters, uncovers particle-attached Pelagibacterales, maps chemolithoautotrophy and biosynthetic gene clusters, and identifies a rhodopsin clade specific to the dark ocean.

papers.title: Programmed ribosomal frameshifting triggers translational stress to promote viral replication
papers.summary: Viruses such as SARS-CoV-2 can use programmed ribosomal frameshifting to turn off host translation and promote viral replication, expanding the known uses of programmed ribosomal frameshifting by viruses.

papers.title: Norway spruce spatiotemporal programs of conifer reproductive development
papers.summary: Spatiotemporal transcriptomics across conifer reproductive and vegetative shoots reveals candidate developmental regulators and evolutionarily conserved tissue patterning genes in seed plants.

papers.title: Copper ion-induced MYH9 polymerization executes cuproptosis
papers.summary: Copper binding drives MYH9 polymerization, triggering cytoskeletal collapse and cuproptosis. HThPA releases intracellular copper through glutathione depletion, exposing a therapeutic vulnerability in drug-resistant tumors.

papers.title: Metax enables accurate cross-domain taxonomic profiling of metagenomes
papers.summary: Metax is a cross-domain metagenomic profiler that uses genome-wide coverage evidence to improve species-level microbial profiling and distinguish supported taxa from artifacts. Across diverse datasets, Metax enables robust taxonomic profiling, pathogen detection, contamination assessment, and discovery of disease-associated bacterial and viral signatures.

papers.title: Mitochondrial ATP promotes T cell differentiation through chromatin accessibility
papers.summary: Cell-mediated immunity requires cytotoxic CD8+ T cells that adopt and maintain an effector phenotype. Here, D-α-hydroxybutyrate (DAHB) is shown to act as a metabolic adjuvant, driving the conversion of proliferating CD8+ T cells into cytotoxic effector cells by linking mitochondrial ATP production to chromatin remodeling and gene expression.

papers.title: Glycocalyx-edited mesenchymal stem/stromal cell therapy in advanced osteoporosis
papers.summary: Mesenchymal stem/stromal cell (MSC)-based therapy holds promise for reversal of bone loss in osteoporosis. This phase 1 study establishes the safety and feasibility of intravenous administration of glycocalyx-engineered human MSCs and provides evidence that MSCs derived from the bone marrow of older individuals with osteoporosis retain clinically meaningful osteoregenerative capacity.

papers.title: Native pathogen-phage networks reveal multilayered defense and gut-active anti-phage immunity
papers.summary: Wang et al. map >1,000 interactions between Salmonella isolates and bacteriophages to measure the relative contributions of surface features and intracellular defense to phage resistance across a major human pathogen. They further identify AppA, which blocks DNA packaging by targeting the large terminase and restricts phage replication within mammalian hosts.

papers.title: Within-host evolution and transmission of a human gut symbiont across ecological scales
papers.summary: Vasquez et al. use high-resolution lineage tracking to follow tens of thousands of Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron lineages in the mouse gut. They show that rapid evolution can overcome colonization resistance, enabling adaptive strains to spread between hosts, while community diversity reshapes the evolutionary landscape without preventing adaptation and transmission.

papers.title: An enzyme-responsive nanoplatform rewires host-microbe tryptophan metabolism for cancer immunotherapy
papers.summary: An oral enzyme-responsive co-delivery nanoplatform is designed to achieve controlled release of tryptophan and the metabolism inhibitor NLG919, specifically in the large intestine. This design redirects tryptophan metabolism toward immunostimulatory microbial indole derivative production, while blocking the immunosuppressive kynurenine pathway, thereby synergistically eliciting robust antitumor immunity in colorectal cancer.

papers.title: Myo-inositol metabolism counteracts mycotoxin hijacking and confers broad resistance to fungal diseases in crops
papers.summary: Xia et al. reveal that the Fusarium mycotoxin DON hijacks host central metabolism through NAD+-dependent enzymes to promote disease and identify MIPS as a key safeguard that redirects myo-inositol metabolism to drive PI(4,5)P2-dependent vacuolar sequestration of DON, maintaining metabolic homeostasis and conferring broad Fusarium resistance in crops.

papers.title: A commensal-derived sugar protects against obesity by regulating immunometabolism
papers.summary: Tan et al. identify a human commensal bacterium, Clostridium immunis—and its bioactive phosphocholine-modified exopolysaccharide (EPS)—that reduces visceral adiposity and weight gain in mice. By decreasing IL-22 levels, this EPS increases metabolic activity specifically in visceral fat. Metagenomic analyses suggest that this bacterial pathway may be conserved in humans.

papers.title: Dietary pectin remodels commensal bacterial surfaces to promote IgA-mediated protection from intestinal inflammation
papers.summary: Tang et al. reveal that dietary pectin drives Bacteroides uniformis surface remodeling to enrich the surface glycosphingolipid HexCer. Neutrophils sense this signal via CLEC4E to promote IgA production, which helps this bacterium colonize the gut lining and protects against colitis, uncovering a diet-microbe pathway that promotes a mutually beneficial relationship.

papers.title: Lymphatic constraint of germinal centers optimizes protective antibody responses
papers.summary: Lymphatic vessel networks remodel during infection to regulate antigen and immune cell dynamics, yet whether these changes impact humoral immunity remains unknown. Mudianto et al. demonstrate that lymph node lymphangiogenesis encapsulates activating germinal centers to constrain their size, which enhances clonal selection and protective antibody responses, establishing lymphatic vessels as structural determinants of germinal center fitness.

papers.title: Single-cell analyses of global cohorts outline determinants of immune aging and link the ratio of GZMK+ to GZMB+ Tem cells to health trajectories
papers.summary: Terekhova et al. assemble a single-cell PBMC atlas of 8 datasets, 2,609 individuals, and over 12 million cells to dissect variable and conserved features of human immune aging. CD8+ Tem GZMK+ to GZMB+ ratio distinguishes healthy from disease-associated trajectories and predicts mortality risk. This work provides a clinically relevant marker for monitoring human aging.

papers.title: Microglia-mediated extracellular matrix disruption drives neuronal dysfunction, motor impairments, and sedation following alcohol abuse
papers.summary: Alcohol’s brain effects are attributed to neurons, leaving microglial functional involvement untested. Paouri, Stanko, et al. show that microglia drive alcohol-induced sedation, motor impairment, and synaptic and neuronal loss through MyD88-dependent perisynaptic extracellular matrix (ECM) disruption. Equivalent neuron-targeted sedation bypassing microglia spares the ECM. Brain ECM loss also marks human alcohol use disorder, identifying a therapeutic target distinct from neuronal interventions.

papers.title: Induced regulatory B cells stably expressing interleukin-10 reverse central nervous system autoimmunity by targeting myeloid cells
papers.summary: Interleukin (IL)-10 produced by B cells has regulatory functions in disease contexts. Manfroi et al. report a strategy for the efficient generation of IL-10-producing B cells using a chemical compound identified through a high-throughput screen. Upon transfer, these IL-10+ B cells reverse ongoing CNS autoimmunity at disease peak in a manner dependent on IL-10 receptor expression in myeloid cells.

papers.title: Distant lymph nodes compensate for resected tumor-draining lymph nodes during cancer immunotherapy
papers.summary: Menzel, Zhou, et al. examine the impact of surgical removal of tumor-draining lymph node (tdLN) resection on anti-tumor immunity. They find that after tdLN resection, tumor antigen is rerouted to distant LNs, where it supports tumor-specific T cell responses and immune checkpoint blockade efficacy. Targeting these compensatory LNs enhances anti-cancer immunity after lymph node surgery.

papers.title: Functional evaluation of TCR-pMHC pairs at scale allows in silico TCR reactivity prediction
papers.summary: Messemaker et al. develop a TCR rapid assembly platform (T-RAP) and use it to generate a large high-quality dataset of functionally validated TCR-pMHC pairs. With the resulting validated TCR-pMHC dataset (TCRvdb), structure-based prediction of TCR-pMHC reactivity is more feasible than previously assumed.

papers.title: Glucose-deprived tumor microenvironment activates AMP-activated protein kinase to drive adoptively transferred T helper 9 cell senescence
papers.summary: Glucose deprivation in the solid tumor microenvironment impairs T cell persistence, but the mechanisms remain unclear. Fu et al. identified an AMPK-ZAK-NIK axis activated by glucose deprivation in Th9 cells that inhibits IL-9 secretion, triggering cell senescence and impaired persistence. ZAK targeting rejuvenates Th9 cells, consequently boosting the anti-tumor potency of CAR-Th9-based therapies for solid tumors.

papers.title: Influenza vaccine format mediates distinct cellular and antibody responses in human immune organoids
Aire is a cell-intrinsic regulator of natural IgM-secreting cells
papers.summary: The autoimmune regulator (Aire) promotes T cell tolerance through promiscuous gene expression in medullary thymic epithelial cells, but growing evidence suggests that it has functions beyond its canonical role in thymic tolerance. Sayed et al. demonstrate that Aire acts as a cell-intrinsic regulator of T-independent natural IgM-secreting cells, homeostatically restraining their number and natural IgM abundance.

papers.title: Microglia with distinct origins and non-canonical phenotypes coexist within the border-like niche of the brain’s circumventricular organs
papers.summary: Circumventricular organs are specialized brain regions lacking a blood-brain barrier. Van Hove et al. reveal that these regions harbor unique microglia and border-associated macrophage populations that respond to ageing and metabolism and are partly derived from fetal monocytes entering during a perinatal window, which can fully adopt the microglia identity.

papers.title: Targeting a site of vulnerability on circumsporozoite protein inhibits Plasmodium vivax malaria infection
papers.summary: Limited knowledge of protective B cell epitopes on the Plasmodium vivax circumsporozoite protein (PvCSP) remains a roadblock to vaccine development. Visweswaran et al. identify an inhibitory vaccine epitope on PvCSP that elicits antibodies capable of blocking sporozoite invasion of host hepatocytes. Definition of the structural basis for epitope recognition by a neutralizing antibody provides a roadmap for vaccine design.

papers.title: Germinal center interleukin-4 microniches drive tissue divergence of IgE memory B cell responses
papers.summary: IgE recall responses sustain allergic disease, but their anatomical regulation remains poorly understood. Villazala-Merino et al. identify Tfh cell-derived IL-4 microniches within germinal centers as an anatomical checkpoint that favors IgE recall responses in lymphoid organs while limiting their generation in the lung mucosa.

papers.title: Sensory neuronal mTORC1 kinase signaling establishes neuroimmune memory that initiates allergic immunity
papers.summary: How cumulative environmental allergen exposures are encoded by peripheral sensory neurons to shape immune responsiveness is unclear. Zhu et al. show that protease allergens induce an mTORC1-dependent, metabolically trained state in sensory neurons that amplifies later neuroimmune responses to allergens and enables cross-sensitization to antigenically distinct allergens.

papers.title: Cancers modulate processing and presentation of p53 neoantigens to evade T cell detection
papers.summary: Mutations in TP53 occur early in malignant transformation and are generally present in all descendant tumor cells. Haratani et al. find a dearth of actionable neoantigens displayed in the cancer immunopeptidome and define various mechanisms whereby tumor cells prevent effective processing and presentation of p53 neoantigens.

papers.title: More Microplastics and Nanoplastics Detected in Patients With Heart Attacks
papers.summary: More microplastics and nanoplastics have been found in the coronary circulation of patients experiencing ST-elevation myocardial infarctions (STEMIs) compared with blood from healthy coronary arteries or those with chronic coronary syndromes.

papers.title: Nicotine Vapes May Aid in Smoking Cessation
papers.summary: More people may quit smoking when using nicotine e-cigarettes, also known as vapes, compared with conventional nicotine replacement therapies (NRT) such as gum or patches and quitting with or without behavioral support, according to an updated Cochrane review.

papers.title: Study Finds Artery Damage in Young Adults With CKM Syndrome
papers.summary: Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome is prevalent among young adults and is associated with greater signs of early artery damage, according to a study published in Circulation: Population Health and Outcomes. Nearly 80% of participants had CKM syndrome stages 1 to 3, which were linked to worse cardiovascular health.

papers.title: Limited Early-Life Sugar Intake Linked to Lower Dementia Risk
papers.summary: People who experienced sugar rationing in their first 1000 days of life had more favorable brain health and lower dementia risk with later onset, an analysis in Neurology suggests.

papers.title: Writing Style May Explain Patient Message Response Disparities
papers.summary: Bias in writing style explained nearly half of disparities in care team replies to patient portal messages from historically marginalized groups, according to a study published in JAMA Network Open.

papers.title: Transfusion Reactions After Tick Bites May Be a New Alpha-Gal Manifestation
papers.summary: Alpha-gal syndrome (AGS), a tick bite−related condition causing red meat allergy through IgE antibody production, may increase risk of allergic reactions to certain blood products, according to a study published in JAMA Internal Medicine. The authors suggest this supports a new clinical entity: transfusion-related AGS (TRAGS), potentially caused by AGS IgE antibodies and transfused B antigens cross-reacting.

papers.title: A New Definition of MI and More News From ESC Congress 2026
papers.summary: This Medical News article is an interview with Tomasz Guzik, MD, PhD, chair of this year’s European Society of Cardiology Congress, held recently in Munich, Germany.

papers.title: Patient Information: Psilocybin
papers.summary: This JAMA Patient Page describes the psychedelic compound psilocybin, its medical and recreational use, and its potential side effects.

papers.title: Psilocybin
papers.summary: This JAMA Insights discusses the medical use of psilocybin, particularly for depression treatment, including emerging potential indications, safety, and future use.

papers.title: From Aging to AI and Beyond
papers.summary: Editor in Chief of JAMA+ AI Roy Perlis, MD, MSc, and Eric Topol, MD, a cardiologist and the founder and director of the Scripps Research Translational Institute, discussed how questions surrounding aging also resonate for AI for the JAMA+ AI Conversations podcast.

papers.title: It Shouldn’t Be Brave
papers.summary: In this narrative medicine essay, an anesthesiologist who has depression longs for the medical community not to think him brave for being open about it but rather think about a need for psychiatric help as being as mundane as filling gas in one’s car.

papers.title: Lessons From the World Trade Center Health Program
papers.summary: This Perspective explores key developments in care delivery and clinical understanding of the population exposed to the 9/11 terrorist attacks through data from the World Trade Center Health Program.

papers.summary: Premature menopause may be associated with increased hypertension risk, a study found.

papers.title: FDA Authorizes First Autonomous Robotic Blood Draw Device
papers.summary: The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) authorized the first stand-alone robotic blood draw device for use in adults in an outpatient setting.

papers.title: Colorectal Cancer Deaths Increase Among Younger Adults
papers.summary: Deaths from most leading cancer types have decreased among individuals younger than 50 years, but deaths from colorectal cancer have increased, according to a research letter published in JAMA Network Open.

papers.title: Recent Studies of Modifiable Risk Factors Show Promise for Preventing Dementia
papers.summary: This Medical News article discusses research on modifiable risk factors that could protect against Alzheimer disease and other dementias.

papers.title: Trials Test Phage Therapy for UTIs
papers.summary: This Medical News article discusses recently launched clinical trials of bacteriophage therapy for recurrent and multidrug-resistant urinary tract infections (UTIs).

Everyone Will Feel the $1 Trillion Cut in Medicaid
papers.summary: Proposed Medicaid cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and how they could affect patients, clinicians, and health care organizations are discussed by Derek C. Angus, MD, MPH, and Julie Donohue, PhD, professor and chair of health policy and management at the University of Pittsburgh, on this episode of the Healthy Dialogue podcast.

papers.title: The Pragmatic Clinical Trial
papers.summary: What makes a clinical trial a pragmatic trial? Since the concept of pragmatic trial research was introduced nearly 60 years ago, this label has been applied and interpreted beyond its original meaning. Pragmatic trials were once proposed as alternatives to explanatory studies aimed at establishing the biophysiological effects of medical therapies, often in artificial settings, in narrow patient populations, or in comparison with alternatives that did not exist in routine care. Pragmatic trials were instead conceived as generating more relevant evidence of treatment effects under everyday conditions faced by clinicians and patients, thus providing more applicable insight into whether and how interventions should be adopted in routine practice.

papers.title: Pine, Arizona
papers.summary: Rim Country at eventide: the slight bergamot of sky, a slow diffusion of ink across a canvas

papers.title: “Pills You Can’t Stomach”: Poetry, Medicine, and Resisting Metaphor
papers.summary: In most lyric poetry, of which “Pine, Arizona” is a fine example, such artful devices as metaphor are typically present. Yet when the lyric’s subject is medical, the poem can become an argument between beauty and reality. Lovely details, such as the fading colors of the evening sky and the ethereal singing of unseen coyotes, verge on metaphor yet resist its full embrace, as the spell is broken by a more unpoetic list of stark medical concerns: “The chemotherapy injections//you get in your abdomen. Pills you can’t stomach./Swelling from steroids. A frame irradiated,//and the ache of it all.” Thus the speaker struggles with whether even the impulse to make art can coexist with the blatant, bleak truths of a body wracked with pain and debilitated by both mortal illness and the adverse effects of its treatment. The longing for the possibility of healing through creative self-expression, suggested from the poem’s outset by the quiet pun of its title but never fully satisfied here, reminds u

papers.title: The Veteran Affairs’ Approach for Chronic Pain Management
papers.summary: To the Editor Chronic pain trials increasingly enroll populations with substantial psychiatric symptoms, yet suicidality is often treated as a safety observation rather than a clinically meaningful outcome. The Whole Health Options and Pain Education (wHOPE) trial illustrates this tension. Despite exclusion of patients with active suicidality at baseline, suicidal ideation was the most common adverse event, occurring in 13.7% of the whole health group, 15.9% of the cognitive behavior therapy group, and 13.4% of the usual care group, with no differential reduction by intervention. Together, these findings reflect that suicidal ideation in people with chronic pain is often documented for safety surveillance but not evaluated as a pain-linked clinical outcome.

papers.title: The Veteran Affairs’ Approach for Chronic Pain Management—Reply
papers.summary: In Reply We thank Drs Mendes Neto and Mendes for their letter about the wHOPE trial. We agree there is a blind spot in addressing the relationship between chronic pain and psychological conditions, including suicidal ideation, and the need to assess suicidal ideation and behaviors as clinical outcomes in trials of patients with chronic pain. In addition, trials are needed that enroll individuals with co-occurring chronic pain and mental health conditions, including suicidal ideation, to rigorously evaluate integrated interventions that address pain and mood.

papers.title: Parental Support Package for Pregnant and Postpartum Trainees
papers.summary: To the Editor The recent article on a pragmatic parental support package to mitigate burnout among pregnant and postpartum trainees addressed a real and underrecognized problem. However, the proposed parental support package did not address the structural determinants of burnout in this population, and framing it as a meaningful solution risks diverting attention from reforms with greater demonstrated impact.

papers.title: Parental Support Package for Pregnant and Postpartum Trainees—Reply
papers.summary: In Reply We share the conviction of Dr Patek and colleagues that parental leave is critically important for the well-being of childbearing trainees. We believe, however, that burnout among childbearing trainees is multifactorial, and the empirical evidence does not support paid parental leave as the single most important intervention to reduce burnout in this population. While foundational, leave policies do not address many stressors that emerge during pregnancy or after trainees return to clinical work. As Patek and colleagues note, regardless of leave duration, trainees ultimately transition back to work, and support is needed when they do.

papers.title: Amoxicillin-Clavulanate vs Amoxicillin for Sinusitis

These findings are important for antimicrobial stewardship and support narrower-spectrum therapy when antibiotics are indicated for uncomplicated acute sinusitis.

The decision to randomize patients to adjuvant embolization after surgical drainage is commendable because it preserves blinding of the surgeon and isolates the effect of embolization from variability in surgical performance.

papers.title: Iron Delivery Amid Nutritional and Infectious Adversity
papers.summary: Providing sufficient iron for brain development while protecting children from infection in malaria-endemic areas has remained an unresolved public health goal for more than 2 decades. A landmark study conducted on Pemba Island, Tanzania, brought the complex relationship between iron and malaria to the forefront by demonstrating that universal prophylactic iron supplementation increased the risk of hospitalization and death among young children in areas of high malaria transmission. Subsequent analyses suggested that the risk was concentrated among iron-replete rather than iron-deficient children. Preventing iron deficiency and maintaining an adequate supply of iron to the brain during the first 1000 days of life is likely far more effective than remediation after iron deficiency occurs. Even transient iron deficiency during critical developmental windows may produce long-lasting alterations in brain development and function.

papers.title: Defining Amyloid Positivity on the Centiloid Scale
papers.summary: Amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) plays a central role in both Alzheimer disease research and clinical care by enabling in vivo detection of cerebral amyloid-β deposition, one of the core pathological features of this disease. Over the past 2 decades, amyloid PET has transformed understanding of the natural history of Alzheimer disease and has had a pivotal role in patient selection and as a secondary outcome for clinical trials—ultimately paving the way for US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval of amyloid-targeting therapies as the first class of disease-modifying therapies. Clinically, amyloid PET can be used to support diagnosis in patients with mild cognitive impairment or diagnostically uncertain cognitive syndromes. More recently, it is being used to establish the presence of amyloid plaques prior to initiating amyloid-targeting therapies and as part of evaluating the therapeutic response.

papers.title: A semi-automated tool for improving Assessments and Lab Tests data annotation in ImmPort
papers.summary: Public data sharing in immunological and clinical research is essential for transparency, reproducibility, and secondary analysis. However, many datasets in repositories such as ImmPort lack sufficient structured data to enable reuse. ImmPort's Assessments and Lab Tests templates -- which capture critical clinical information -- are often incomplete or omitted due to their complexity and the manual effort required. To address this challenge, an application with a graphical user interface requiring no programming was developed to facilitate population of these templates. The tool streamlines the submission process by reducing time and complexity for data contributors while ensuring template formatting. It integrates ImmPort files, study-specific data files, and a curated data dictionary to automate the mapping of study variables to the required fields within each template. papers.title: Restoration of deficient IL-15 signaling enhances innate lymphoid cell immunity in brain metastasis
papers.summary: Natural killer (NK) cells and type 1 innate lymphoid cells (ILC1s), collectively known as group 1 innate lymphoid cells (ILCs), are critical mediators of anti-tumor immunity, yet their role in brain metastasis remains poorly defined. Using single-cell RNA sequencing and functional depletion models, we show that group 1 ILCs fail to provide adequate tumor control in breast cancer brain metastasis (BCBM). In contrast to the liver, where diverse, functionally competent group 1 ILC populations facilitate excellent metastatic control, group 1 ILCs in BCBM show limited diversity and profound tissue-specific dysfunction such that their depletion had no effect on tumor burden despite modest parenchymal infiltration. We attribute this group 1 ILC dysfunction to severely restricted IL-15 availability, with IL-15R protein detected at 500-fold lower concentration in the brain than in the liver. papers.title: A mast cell receptor is associated with fibrosis and itch in systemic sclerosis
papers.summary: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is an autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by symmetric fibrosis of the skin and multiple internal organs. The mechanisms that trigger early fibrotic changes remain unclear. Mast cells are known to infiltrate human SSc lesional skin in early disease stages, yet the role of mast cells in initiating fibrosis and pruritus in SSc remains debated, in part due to unclear pathways of mast cell activation. Here, we show that mast cells, via the receptor Mrgprb2, contribute to fibrosis in the bleomycin (BLM)-induced skin fibrosis mouse model. Mast cells accumulate in the skin of BLM-treated wild-type (WT) but not Mrgprb2-knockout (Mrgprb2-/-) mice. Mrgprb2-/- mice show attenuated disease severity, with reduced collagen deposition and lower expression of matrix metalloproteinases and inflammatory markers associated with fibrosis. papers.title: The transition to postpartum lactation establishes a state of maternal antiviral resilience
papers.summary: Influenza A virus (IAV) causes severe disease during late pregnancy, yet how maternal adaptations in host defense shape susceptibility following childbirth remains unknown. Here, we show that the postpartum period represents a state of enhanced maternal antiviral immunity. Across postpartum stages, dams infected before weaning exhibited increased survival and reduced disease following lethal IAV challenge compared with nonpregnant females. Postpartum protection was associated with enhanced viral clearance and increased pulmonary antigen-specific CD8+ T cells and IL-17A-producing gamma-delta T cells. We identify the transition into lactation as a critical determinant of this protection. Protection extended to highly pathogenic avian influenza. Together, these findings reveal that maternal antiviral immunity remains actively shaped after childbirth, establishing the postpartum lactational period as a distinct state of maternal antiviral resilience.

papers.title: Phenuivirus glycoprotein Gc domain is a conserved target of cross-functional monoclonal antibodies
papers.summary: Phenuiviruses which include Rift Valley Fever Virus (RVFV), classified by WHO as one of the top priority pathogens with outbreak potential, are emerging arthropod-borne viruses that pose an increasing threat to public health. In line with the prototype pathogen framework advanced by the NIAID, the sandfly-transmitted Toscana virus (TOSV) has been adopted as a prototype to advance understanding of relevant phenuiviruses and inform the development of broadly applicable medical countermeasures. In this study, we sought to isolate and characterize monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) elicited by natural TOSV infection to identify shared antigenic determinants. By employing the conserved envelope Gc glycoprotein as bait for antigen-specific B cell sorting, we recovered more than 1,450 memory B cells and identified 112 Gc-specific neutralizing mAbs. Over one-third of these mAbs exhibited cross-reactivity with RVFV, a genetically distinct phenuivirus. Selected mAbs provided prophylactic protection in

papers.title: Time-Evolving Immunomodulatory Activity in Green-Fixed Devitalized Cellular Materials
papers.summary: By decoupling biological function from cellular viability, fixed abiotic cellular materials have emerged as a promising platform for next-generation immunotherapies, preserving essential immunomodulatory activities while enabling unprecedented control over manufacturing, storage, and standardization. Nevertheless, the coupled effects of fabrication history and post-fabrication environmental cues on their biological functionality remain elusive. Here, we show that both preparation route and storage time critically affect the bioactivity of mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC)-derived microtissues. By exploring different devitalization agents, we demonstrate that an ethanol-based strategy provides a green fixation option with comparable preservation of volumetric and fixed cell architecture, as well as immunomodulatory function. Processing protocols did not merely substitute conventional fixation but tailored specific immune-related bioactivity. An unexpected processing protocol and time-depen

papers.title: Promyelocytic leukemia (PML) suppresses hepatitis B virus cccDNA transcription through SUMOylation- and SMC5/6-dependent mechanisms
papers.summary: Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection persists under current antiviral therapy because covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) remains in the infected hepatocytes as a durable transcriptional template. Although type I interferon (IFN-I) can reduce HBV cccDNA gene expression, the host effectors and mechanisms that restrict cccDNA remain incompletely defined. Using a minicircle-based HBV cccDNA expressing a Gaussia luciferase reporter gene (mcHBV-GLuc), we investigated how promyelocytic leukemia protein (PML) suppresses HBV cccDNA activity. Multiple PML isoforms reduced cccDNA-driven reporter activity and HBsAg production, and HBx-deficient ({Delta}X) mcHBV cccDNA was more susceptible than wild-type cccDNA to PML-mediated inhibition. Interestingly, efficient antiviral activity required the major PML SUMOylation sites. papers.title: A moonlighting serpin of Tannerella forsythia compromises the bactericidal activity of neutrophils
papers.summary: Serine protease inhibitors (serpins) are extremely rare in prokaryotes, and their role in immune evasion remains unclear. We identified a bifunctional TLR2-binding serpin (miropin) produced by Tannerella forsythia that broadly suppresses neutrophil antimicrobial capacity. Miropin binding to TLR2 primed neutrophils, enhancing phagocytic capacity yet, counterintuitively, promoting bacterial persistence. Mechanistically, like other serpins, miropin acted as an irreversible suicide inhibitor of neutrophil serine proteases (NSPs), blocking their activity upon granule mobilization and NETosis. Unexpectedly, miropin, independent of its protease-inhibitory activity, bound and inhibited myeloperoxidase (MPO), thereby blocking the oxidative burst. This simultaneous suppression of oxidative and non-oxidative bactericidal mechanisms promoted bacterial survival in vivo without significantly altering the tissue inflammatory response. papers.title: Repeated malaria exposure reprograms Vδ2+ γδT cell chromatin accessibility and immune function toward a reversible hyporesponsive state
papers.summary: V{delta}2+ {gamma}{delta} T cells contribute to antimalarial immunity via pro-inflammatory and cytotoxic mechanisms. Among children who have experienced repeated episodes of malaria, V{delta}2+ T cells develop reduced pro-inflammatory function through mechanisms that remain unknown. We hypothesized that recurrent malaria drives coordinated epigenetic and transcriptional remodeling of these semi-innate cells. Using PBMC from Ugandan children in cohorts spanning high and low transmission (10 children) and longitudinally across a marked decline in transmission (20 children, 3 timepoints), we profiled the epigenome and transcriptome of V{delta}2+ T cells by paired bulk ATAC-seq and RNA-seq and by CITE-seq. Higher malaria exposure was associated with reduced V{delta}2+ T cell TNF and IFN{gamma} production and with thousands of differentially accessible chromatin regions. Immunoregulatory genes including LYN, PLCG2, and HAVCR2 (Tim-3) showed increased chromatin accessibility and/or expressio

papers.title: Fatty acid metabolism and dietary lipid composition shape B-cell responses
papers.summary: B-cell activation requires extensive metabolic reprogramming, yet how B cells acquire and utilize extracellular fatty acids and adapt to changes in lipid availability remains poorly understood. Here, we show that B-cell activation and the extracellular lipid environment dynamically regulate B cells. B-cell receptor (BCR) and Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) stimulation induced distinct mitochondrial and lipid-handling programs, differentially regulating fatty-acid uptake, cholesterol acquisition, lipid storage and mitochondrial respiration. Disrupting long-chain fatty-acid uptake, acyl-CoA activation, or mitochondrial utilisation impaired B-cell proliferation, demonstrating that multiple steps of fatty-acid metabolism are required for B-cell expansion. However, increasing extracellular fatty-acid availability alone did not enhance proliferation, indicating that fatty-acid acquisition and metabolic utilisation are functionally distinct. papers.title: A PATHOGENIC NFKB2 VARIANT CAUSES COMBINED IMMUNODEFICIENCY WITH THYMIC AND PERIPHERAL LYMPHOID DEFECTS IN RATS
papers.summary: The non-canonical NF-kappa B pathway, in which NFKB2 plays a central role, is critical for lymphoid organ development and immune homeostasis. Pathogenic NFKB2 variants have been strongly associated with a broad spectrum of human pathologies, notably immunodysregulation syndromes, characterized by recurrent infections, autoantibody production and endocrine abnormalities. The mechanisms underlying the resulting immune defects remain incompletely understood. In the present study, we characterized the immune phenotype of a novel rat model harboring a Nfkb2 non-sense mutation located in the c-terminal region of the gene (c.2602T>A; p.Tyr867*, Nfkb2p.Tyr867*). This variant has been identified in patients with a familial form of common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) presenting with autoimmunity manifestations. papers.title: Lactation Remodels the Maternal Lung to Promote Preemptive Innate Defense
papers.summary: Lactation is a hallmark of mammalian evolution, imposing extraordinary physiological demands on mothers to nourish their offspring. Yet how mothers maintain their own health while meeting these demands remains poorly understood. Here, we discover that lactation establishes a preemptive innate defense program in the maternal lung through enhanced epithelial production of surfactant proteins and mucin, vascular remodeling that supports granulocyte recruitment and accumulation of activated intravascular neutrophils. These tissue-wide adaptations safeguard lactating dams against diverse respiratory pathogens. We further identify prolactin and CGRP as neuroendocrine signals contributing to pulmonary remodeling and uncover parallel lactation-associated granulocyte adaptations in marsupial and non-human primate models. Together, our findings expand the framework of reproductive immunology, revealing that reproduction couples systemic fetal tolerance with tissue-specific immune adaptations tha

papers.title: Age-associated transcriptional programs in tumor-associated macrophages are associated with tumor progression in HPV-negative oral cancer
papers.summary: Aging and tobacco exposure are major determinants of risk and outcome in HPV-negative oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), yet the cellular programs linking host factors to tumor immunity remain poorly defined. We reprocessed and reanalyzed previously published single-cell RNA-seq data from 19 HPV-negative OSCC tumors and we identified a robust age- and smoking-associated expansion of SPP1high tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), accompanied by a shift toward a myeloid-dominant and lymphocyte-reduced tumor microenvironment. SPP1high TAMs exhibit a distinct transcriptional state enriched for extracellular-matrix remodeling and metabolic programs and reduced antigen-presentation pathways. They also express inflammatory chemokines such as CXCL2 and CXCL3 and down-regulate the cytotoxic mediator TNFSF10, suggesting a broadly protumor TAM phenotype. Ligand-receptor modeling suggests that SPP1high TAMs act as key communication hubs, with dominant SPP1-CD44 signaling to T-cell subsets.

papers.title: The MRTFs are required for thymocyte trafficking and Treg-mediated immune tolerance
papers.summary: The MRTFs (myocardin-related transcription factors) are essential for effective cytoskeletal function during differentiation and development. To investigate the role played by the MRTFs in T cell development and function we inactivated Mrtfb in Mrtfa-null mice at the DN2 stage (MrtfabKOT animals). Positive selection, and development of MrtfabKOT regulatory (Treg), {gamma}{delta}, and NK T cells proceeded normally. Thymic egress was impaired, however, with mature T cells accumulating at the cortico-medullary junction, and in vitro MrtfabKOT thymocytes exhibited impaired cytoskeletal responses to S1P and migratory cytokines. MrtfabKOT mice were lymphopenic, with defective homeostatic proliferation and T cell homing to peripheral lymphoid organs. Although thymocyte negative selection was unaffected, MrtfabKOT animals develop autoimmune phenotypes in lacrimal gland and intestinal mucosa. papers.title: PPARγ brakes cytosolic DNA-induced macrophage inflammation by super-enhancer metabolic reprogramming
papers.summary: Cytoplasmic DNA sensing triggers intense innate immune responses that require tight regulation. PPAR{gamma} is a master metabolic regulator in macrophages, but its role in cytoplasmic DNA immunity remains unclear. Using poly(dA:dT) to mimic cytoplasmic DNA stimulation, we combined transcriptomics, epigenomics (PPAR{gamma}/H3K27ac ChIP-seq), and functional assays. Poly(dA:dT) induced a cytokine storm with MAPK activation and apoptosis/necrosis. PPAR{gamma} activation by rosiglitazone (RGZ) antagonized this response, reducing cell death and transcriptionally inhibiting MAPK genes (e.g., DUSP4/10). Mechanistically, PPAR{gamma} bound promoters/enhancers via PPRE motifs and distal intergenic regions, remodeling H3K27ac (reduced at inflammatory loci, increased at metabolic genes). papers.title: A signaling-optimized TIGIT chimeric switch receptor promotes metabolic fitness and antitumor efficacy of TCR/CAR T cells
papers.summary: Adoptive T cell therapies have revolutionized the treatment of hematological malignancies, however, their efficacy against solid tumors often remains limited. Lack of activation and overabundance of immune checkpoint-mediated inhibitory signals from cancer cells drive T cell dysfunction and limit persistence. To circumvent this imbalance towards inhibitory factors, we engineered a chimeric switch receptor (CSR) that repurposes the immunosuppressive TIGIT extracellular domain by fusing it to a CD28-derived stimulatory signaling tail. Here we show that while the prototype CSR design enhances immediate cytolytic activity, it also induces premature proliferative arrest and terminal differentiation due to excessive tonic signaling. By introducing a strategic point mutation within the CD28 cytoplasmic domain, we "fine-tuned" the activation threshold of the CSR for optimal functional properties. papers.title: Immune determinants of leuprolide-associated cardiovascular risk in prostate cancer
papers.summary: Leuprolide, a widely used androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT) for prostate cancer (PC), has been associated with increased cardiovascular events (CVE), although the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Through integrated spatial transcriptomic analyses of murine heart and immune-stromal profiling in patient blood, we identified immune programs linked to leuprolide-associated CVE risk. Spatial analyses revealed the distinct organization of lymphoid (T+B cells) aggregates and inflammatory macrophages in the plaque following leuprolide exposure that accompanied by ventricular hypertrophy, relative to normal vasculature. Parallel profiling of circulatory soluble and cellular components in patients demonstrated CD8+T cell enriched pattern in ~44% of patients, including memory and type 1 cytotoxic subsets that linked to treatment-induced CVE, such as ventricular dysfunctions, but no contribution of adipocytokines. papers.title: DancE: A DNA-Activated Bacterial cGAS-like Enzyme in Antiphage Immune Defense
papers.summary: Vertebrate cGAS senses DNA and synthesizes cyclic GMP-AMP to launch an immune response through the adaptor protein STING. Bacterial cyclic oligonucleotide-based signaling systems (CBASS) are evolutionarily related to the metazoan cGAS-STING pathway, but the molecular cues triggering bacterial cGAS activation remain poorly understood. Here, we identify a cGAS-like enzyme, termed DancE (DNA-activated di-nucleotide cyclase in Escherichia), that is activated by binding to double-stranded DNA. DancE is repressed by the bacterial chaperone DnaK, which prevents DNA binding by DancE. We further identified lambda phage prohead protease gpC that activates DancE through its protease activity. These results provide an example of a bacterial cGAS-like enzyme that is activated by DNA but through a guard-like mechanism that normally suppresses DNA sensing, suggesting that DNA sensing by cGAS family proteins is an ancient antiviral strategy conserved across kingdoms of life.

papers.title: Rhinovirus Infection of Human Airway Epithelial Cells Stimulates Neutrophil Superoxide
papers.summary: Background: Neutrophils migrate to the respiratory epithelium during rhinovirus (RV) infection, but whether RV directly activates neutrophils or whether activation arises from epithelial responses remains unclear. Objective: To determine whether RV directly activates human neutrophils or indirectly activates them through RV infected airway epithelial cells. Methods: Human neutrophils were exposed to purified RV, and activation was assessed by myeloperoxidase activity, CD11b/CD66b expression, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. Neutrophils were co-cultured with RV-infected air liquid interface (ALI) bronchial epithelium evaluated for effects on epithelial integrity. At 48 to 72 hours post-infection, we used live-cell imaging to measure ROS responses and neutrophil-tracking assays to measure migration velocity and ROS responses to basolateral supernatants, clarified apical washes, and apical debris from RV-infected epithelial cells. papers.title: Programmable antigen-presenting scaffolds expand rare tumor-antigen-specific T cells from peripheral blood
papers.summary: Adoptive cellular therapies can be effective against solid tumors but rely on the identification and expansion of rare tumor-reactive T cells (TRTs). Here, we utilize antigen-presenting cell-mimetic scaffolds (APC-ms), a modular biomaterial platform that presents defined peptide-HLA and co-stimulatory ligands on a fluid lipid bilayer to selectively recover rare antigen-specific T cells from peripheral blood. Independent variation of peptide-HLA, co-stimulatory ligands, and cytokine support defined a formulation that enriched MART-1-specific T cells to above 2% of CD8+ T cells in 35 of 50 HLA-A*02:01+ healthy donors from low or undetectable baseline frequencies. Compared with mo-DCs, APC-ms achieved greater fold expansion of MART-1-specific T cells with increased functional avidity and preservation of an early differentiation phenotype, and generated a higher number of MART-1-specific clonotypes. papers.title: Ethmoid bone marrow region modulates lymphoid activation and differentiation with distinct myeloid profile in neuroinflammation
papers.summary: The skull bone marrow axis has recently emerged as an important source of immune cells during neuroinflammation, including in the experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) , the mouse model of multiple sclerosis. The cribriform plate bone marrow (cpBM), is a portion of the ethmoid bone of the skull of mice, and is positioned next to nasal regions. At the cribriform plate olfactory nerves pass through the skull and recent evidence supports that it represents an important immune niche with links to CSF outflow and connections to cpBM. Previous data supports cellular composition of the ethmoid bone marrow in mice is altered in neuroinflammation suggesting it senses inflammatory cues, but the exact nature of these changes is still unclear. Here using scRNAseq and flow cytometry of the ethmoid bone marrow region we test how the region responds to EAE. In addition we also compare the cpBM region with systemic bone marrow in the femur to understand region specific differences. We report

papers.title: Activation of α7 Nicotinic Acetylcholine Receptor Inhibits Neutrophil ex vivo Swarming and Pulmonary Recruitment in Inflamed Mice through an Integrin αMβ2-dependent Mechanism
papers.summary: Background. The cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway regulates inflammation through vagus signaling that activates the 7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (7nAChR) on leukocytes. Suppression of macrophage inflammatory cytokine production through 7nAChR-mediated inhibition of NF-{kappa}B activation is considered a central mechanism of this pathway. However, the effects of cholinergic activation of 7nAChR on neutrophils remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated whether and how activation of 7nAChR in neutrophils regulates neutrophil migration, defined the underlying molecular mechanism, and evaluated its contribution to anti-inflammatory protection during endotoxemia. Results. The ex vivo swarming assays revealed that activation of 7nAChR with the selective agonists PNU-282987 and AR-R17779 significantly inhibited human and mouse neutrophil migration. The inhibitory effect of PNU-282987 was abolished in 7nAChR-deficient neutrophils, confirming receptor specificity. Mechanistically,

papers.title: CD14 Blockade Attenuates Arrhythmogenic Cardiomyopathy
papers.summary: Background: Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM) is a genetic and phenotypically heterogeneous myocardial disorder characterized by progressive cardiomyocyte loss, immune cell infiltration, and fibro-fatty replacement of the ventricular myocardium, with an increased risk of sudden cardiac death (SCD), predominantly caused by mutations in cardiac desmosomal genes including PKP2, DSP, and DSG2. We previously described the pivotal role of NF{kappa}B and CCR2+ cardiac macrophage-triggered inflammation in ACM pathogenesis. Methods: WT or Dsg2mut/mut mice were treated with either isotype control or anti-CD14 antibody once a week for the described treatment period (4 or 8 weeks). At the end of the treatment period, disease characteristics were assessed by echocardiography, electrocardiography, histology, immunofluorescence, positron emission tomography (PET) imaging and single-cell transcriptomics.
